notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0143.stoa002.opp-la: 'senme- . dicaminis' is corrupt; taken as sed ... nihil medicaminis ('but no remedy'). 'ceraque sofivit' is taken as ceraque suffivit, 'fumigated [her] with wax', presumably wax from the tomb; the reading is uncertain.

nodes.text: The wife of our man Serenatus, when she was returning from the farm, her husband having been sent on ahead, suddenly slipped from the hands of those accompanying her and collapsed to the ground; and, her tongue bound, unable to bring any word out of her mouth, she fell mute. Meanwhile soothsayers came, saying that she was suffering the attack of the noonday demon, and they applied bindings of herbs and words of incantations; but they could bring no remedy, as is their way, to the dying woman. And when the household was resounding with mingled wailing, her son ran breathless to our niece Eustenia, announcing that his mother had reached the very end of her life. She came to the sick woman and visited her, and, removing the bindings which the fools had put on, she poured oil from the blessed tomb into her mouth and fumigated [her] with wax. Soon, her speech restored and the deceit of wickedness broken, the sick woman recovered.
